The Siemens chemical vapor deposition approach has been the most common route for solar and semiconductor polysilicon production since its invention in the 1950s. A Siemens chemical vapor deposition chamber is a bell-shaped reaction vessel containing around 36–48 pairs of silicon rods (“filaments”) arranged so the growth of ultrapure silicon occurs equally on each rod. An intricate network of pipelines connects the distillation columns used to refine the trichlorosilane and silicon tetrachloride (SiCl ) chemical intermediates to all the chemical vapor 4 deposition reactors in the factory. Once deposition is finished, the rods are removed from the chemical vapor deposition reactors and broken into smaller chunks for shipping to customers. FBR is the other approach to polysilicon production. Bypassing many steps in the Siemens process, the FBR process goes directly from silicon precursor gases—most commonly silane, SiH (not trichlorosilane)—to granules around 2 mm in diameter (Bernreuter 2012). FBR 4 granules can be used stand-alone to make PV ingots or—more commonly—to increase crucible charge weight by filling in the gaps between much larger polysilicon chunks produced by the Siemens process. The 2025 International Technology Roadmap for Photovoltaic reports a 90% market share for Siemens and 10% market share for FBR in 2024, projecting a 72% share for Siemens and 28% share for FBR in 2035 (Fischer et al. 2025). 33 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.6.2 Domestic Production of Polysilicon PV Tech reported that, in 2024, the United States produced 4.3 GW of polysilicon for the PV dc sector, with a year-end U.S. manufacturing capacity of 39.3 GW , as shown inFigure 23. The dc remaining capacity was idled or used to produce polysilicon for the semiconductor industry. Since 2021, U.S. trade policies against China (e.g., UFLPA) have created a bifurcated market: Japan, Taiwan, and Germany import U.S. polysilicon for semiconductors, and Vietnam—where three of the four largest Chinese PV module companies have set up wafer plants—imports U.S. polysilicon for PV wafers.
